stem: Find the distance between the points P(\(-1\), 1) and Q(5, \(-7\)).
solution:
Suppose co-ordinates of point P are \((x_1, y_1)\) and of point Q are \((x_2, y_2)\).

\(x_1 = -1\),  \(y_1 = 1\),  \(x_2 = 5\),  \(y_2 = -7\)

According to distance formula,

\(d(P, Q) = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{[5 - (-1)]^2 + [(-7) - 1]^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{(6)^2 + (-8)^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{36 + 64}\)

\(d(P, Q) = \sqrt{100} = 10\)

\(\therefore\) distance between points P and Q is 10.

stem: Show that points A(\(-3\), 2), B(1, \(-2\)) and C(9, \(-10\)) are collinear.
solution:
If the sum of any two distances out of \(d(A, B)\), \(d(B, C)\) and \(d(A, C)\) is equal to the third, then the three points A, B and C are collinear.

\(\therefore\) we will find \(d(A, B)\), \(d(B, C)\) and \(d(A, C)\).

Co-ordinates of A are \((-3, 2) = (x_1, y_1)\) and of B are \((1, -2) = (x_2, y_2)\).

\(\therefore d(A, B) = \sqrt{[1 - (-3)]^2 + [(-2) - 2]^2}\)  .......... from distance formula

\(= \sqrt{(1 + 3)^2 + (-4)^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{16 + 16}\)

\(= \sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}\)  ..........(I)

\(d(B, C) = \sqrt{(9 - 1)^2 + (-10 + 2)^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{64 + 64} = 8\sqrt{2}\)  ..........(II)

and \(d(A, C) = \sqrt{(9 + 3)^2 + (-10 - 2)^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{144 + 144} = 12\sqrt{2}\)  ..........(III)

\(\therefore\) from (I), (II) and (III), \(4\sqrt{2} + 8\sqrt{2} = 12\sqrt{2}\)

\(\therefore d(A, B) + d(B, C) = d(A, C)\)

\(\therefore\) Points A, B, C are collinear.

stem: Verify, whether points P(6, \(-6\)), Q(3, \(-7\)) and R(3, 3) are collinear.
solution:
\(PQ = \sqrt{(6 - 3)^2 + (-6 + 7)^2}\)  ..........by distance formula

\(= \sqrt{(3)^2 + (1)^2} = \sqrt{10}\)  .......... (I)

\(QR = \sqrt{(3 - 3)^2 + (-7 - 3)^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{(0)^2 + (-10)^2} = \sqrt{100}\)  .......... (II)

\(PR = \sqrt{(3 - 6)^2 + (3 + 6)^2}\)

\(= \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (9)^2} = \sqrt{90}\)  .......... (III)

From I, II and III out of \(\sqrt{10}\), \(\sqrt{100}\) and \(\sqrt{90}\), \(\sqrt{100}\) is the largest number.

Now we will verify whether \(\left(\sqrt{100}\right)\) and \(\left(\sqrt{10} + \sqrt{90}\right)\) are equal.

For this compare \(\left(\sqrt{100}\right)^2\) and \(\left(\sqrt{10} + \sqrt{90}\right)^2\).

You will see that \(\left(\sqrt{10} + \sqrt{90}\right) > \left(\sqrt{100}\right)\)  \(\therefore\) PQ + PR \(\ne\) QR

\(\therefore\) points P(6, \(-6\)), Q(3, \(-7\)) and R(3, 3) are not collinear.

stem: Show that points (1, 7), (4, 2), (\(-1\), \(-1\)) and (\(-4\), 4) are vertices of a square.
solution:
In a quadrilateral, if all sides are of equal length and both diagonals are of equal length, then it is a square.

\(\therefore\) we will find lengths of sides and diagonals by using the distance formula.

Suppose, A(1, 7), B(4, 2), C(\(-1\), \(-1\)) and D(\(-4\), 4) are the given points.

\(AB = \sqrt{(1 - 4)^2 + (7 - 2)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 25} = \sqrt{34}\)

\(BC = \sqrt{(4 + 1)^2 + (2 + 1)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 9} = \sqrt{34}\)

\(CD = \sqrt{(-1 + 4)^2 + (-1 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 25} = \sqrt{34}\)

\(DA = \sqrt{(1 + 4)^2 + (7 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{25 + 9} = \sqrt{34}\)

\(AC = \sqrt{(1 + 1)^2 + (7 + 1)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 64} = \sqrt{68}\)

\(BD = \sqrt{(4 + 4)^2 + (2 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{64 + 4} = \sqrt{68}\)

\(\therefore\) AB = BC = CD = DA and AC = BD

So, the lengths of four sides are equal and two diagonals are equal.

\(\therefore\) (1, 7), (4, 2), (\(-1\), \(-1\)) and (\(-4\), 4) are the vertices of a square.

stem: Find the co-ordinates of a point on Y-axis which is equidistant from M(\(-5\), \(-2\)) and N(3, 2).
solution:
[Textbook note: the book's last line reads "...are M (0, \(-2\))", but the point it has just found is the one it called P; M is the given point \((-5, -2)\). The co-ordinates \((0, -2)\) are correct; only the label is misprinted.]

Let point P(0, \(y\)) on Y-axis be equidistant from M(\(-5\), \(-2\)) and N(3, 2).

\(\therefore\) PM = PN  \(\therefore\) \(PM^2 = PN^2\)

\(\therefore [0 - (-5)]^2 + [y - (-2)]^2 = (0 - 3)^2 + (y - 2)^2\)

\(\therefore 25 + (y + 2)^2 = 9 + y^2 - 4y + 4\)

\(\therefore 25 + y^2 + 4y + 4 = 13 + y^2 - 4y\)

\(\therefore 8y = -16\)  \(\therefore y = -2\)

\(\therefore\) the co-ordinates of the point on the Y-axis which is equidistant from M and N are \((0, -2)\).
note: The book's closing line prints "M (0, -2)" for the point it has been calling P throughout the solution. Transcribed as printed with an errata bracket; the co-ordinates themselves are correct.

stem: A(\(-3\), \(-4\)), B(\(-5\), 0), C(3, 0) are the vertices of \(\triangle ABC\). Find the co-ordinates of the circumcentre of \(\triangle ABC\).
solution:
Let P(\(a\), b) be the circumcentre of \(\triangle ABC\).

\(\therefore\) point P is equidistant from A, B and C.

\(\therefore PA^2 = PB^2 = PC^2\)  .......... (I)

\(\therefore PA^2 = PB^2\)

\((a + 3)^2 + (b + 4)^2 = (a + 5)^2 + (b - 0)^2\)

\(\therefore a^2 + 6a + 9 + b^2 + 8b + 16 = a^2 + 10a + 25 + b^2\)

\(\therefore -4a + 8b = 0\)

\(\therefore a - 2b = 0\)  .......... (II)

Similarly \(PA^2 = PC^2\)  .......... From (I)

\(\therefore (a + 3)^2 + (b + 4)^2 = (a - 3)^2 + (b - 0)^2\)

\(\therefore a^2 + 6a + 9 + b^2 + 8b + 16 = a^2 - 6a + 9 + b^2\)

\(\therefore 12a + 8b = -16\)

\(\therefore 3a + 2b = -4\)  .......... (III)

Solving (II) and (III) we get \(a = -1\), \(b = -\dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(\therefore\) co-ordinates of circumcentre are \(\left(-1, -\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\).

stem: If point \((x, y)\) is equidistant from points (7, 1) and (3, 5), show that \(y = x - 2\).
solution:
Let point P\((x, y)\) be equidistant from points A(7, 1) and B(3, 5)

\(\therefore\) AP = BP

\(\therefore AP^2 = BP^2\)

\(\therefore (x - 7)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = (x - 3)^2 + (y - 5)^2\)

\(\therefore x^2 - 14x + 49 + y^2 - 2y + 1 = x^2 - 6x + 9 + y^2 - 10y + 25\)

\(\therefore -8x + 8y = -16\)

\(\therefore x - y = 2\)

\(\therefore y = x - 2\)

stem: Find the value of \(y\) if distance between points A(2, \(-2\)) and B(\(-1\), \(y\)) is 5.
solution:
\(AB^2 = [(-1) - 2]^2 + [y - (-2)]^2\)  .......... by distance formula

\(\therefore 5^2 = (-3)^2 + (y + 2)^2\)

\(\therefore 25 = 9 + (y + 2)^2\)

\(\therefore 16 = (y + 2)^2\)

\(\therefore y + 2 = \pm\sqrt{16}\)

\(\therefore y + 2 = \pm 4\)

\(\therefore y = 4 - 2\) or \(y = -4 - 2\)

\(\therefore y = 2\)  or  \(y = -6\)

\(\therefore\) value of \(y\) is 2 or \(-6\).

stem: If A(3, 5), B(7, 9) and point Q divides seg AB in the ratio 2 : 3 then find co-ordinates of point Q.
solution:
In the given example let \((x_1, y_1) = (3, 5)\) and \((x_2, y_2) = (7, 9)\).

\(m : n = 2 : 3\)

According to section formula,

\(x = \dfrac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n} = \dfrac{2 \times 7 + 3 \times 3}{2 + 3} = \dfrac{23}{5}\)

\(y = \dfrac{my_2 + ny_1}{m + n} = \dfrac{2 \times 9 + 3 \times 5}{2 + 3} = \dfrac{33}{5}\)

\(\therefore\) Co-ordinates of Q are \(\left(\dfrac{23}{5}, \dfrac{33}{5}\right)\).

ref: Co-ordinates of the midpoint of a segment SolvedEx.2
stem: Find the co-ordinates of point P if P is the midpoint of a line segment AB with A(\(-4\), 2) and B(6, 2).
solution:
In the given example, suppose \((-4, 2) = (x_1, y_1)\) ; \((6, 2) = (x_2, y_2)\) and co-ordinates of P are \((x, y)\)

\(\therefore\) according to midpoint theorem,

\(x = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2} = \dfrac{-4 + 6}{2} = \dfrac{2}{2} = 1\)

\(y = \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2} = \dfrac{2 + 2}{2} = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2\)

\(\therefore\) co-ordinates of midpoint P are (1, 2).

stem: If point T divides the segment AB with A(\(-7\), 4) and B(\(-6\), \(-5\)) in the ratio 7 : 2, find the co-ordinates of T.
solution:
Let the co-ordinates of T be \((x, y)\).

\(\therefore\) by the section formula,

\(x = \dfrac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n} = \dfrac{7 \times (-6) + 2 \times (-7)}{7 + 2} = \dfrac{-42 - 14}{9} = \dfrac{-56}{9}\)

\(y = \dfrac{my_2 + ny_1}{m + n} = \dfrac{7 \times (-5) + 2 \times (4)}{7 + 2} = \dfrac{-35 + 8}{9} = \dfrac{-27}{9} = -3\)

\(\therefore\) co-ordinates of point T are \(\left(\dfrac{-56}{9}, -3\right)\).

stem: If point P(\(-4\), 6) divides the line segment AB with A(\(-6\), 10) and B(r, s) in the ratio 2 : 1, find the co-ordinates of B.
solution:
By section formula

\(-4 = \dfrac{2 \times r + 1 \times (-6)}{2 + 1}\)

\(\therefore -4 = \dfrac{2r - 6}{3}\)

\(\therefore -12 = 2r - 6\)

\(\therefore 2r = -6\)

\(\therefore r = -3\)

\(6 = \dfrac{2 \times s + 1 \times 10}{2 + 1}\)

\(\therefore 6 = \dfrac{2s + 10}{3}\)

\(\therefore 18 = 2s + 10\)

\(\therefore 2s = 8\)

\(\therefore s = 4\)

\(\therefore\) co-ordinates of point B are \((-3, 4)\).

stem: A(15, 5), B(9, 20) and A\(-\)P\(-\)B. Find the ratio in which point P(11, 15) divides segment AB.
solution:
Suppose, point P(11, 15) divides segment AB in the ratio \(m : n\)

\(\therefore\) by section formula,

\(x = \dfrac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n}\)

\(\therefore 11 = \dfrac{9m + 15n}{m + n}\)

\(\therefore 11m + 11n = 9m + 15n\)

\(\therefore 2m = 4n\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{m}{n} = \dfrac{4}{2} = \dfrac{2}{1}\)

\(\therefore\) The required ratio is 2 : 1.

(The book adds beside this working: "Similarly, find the ratio using \(y\) co-ordinates. Write the conclusion." Doing so gives \(15 = \dfrac{20m + 5n}{m + n}\), so \(15m + 15n = 20m + 5n\), \(10n = 5m\), \(\dfrac{m}{n} = \dfrac{2}{1}\) — the same ratio 2 : 1.)

stem: Find the co-ordinates of the points of trisection of the segment joining the points A(2, \(-2\)) and B(\(-7\), 4). (The two points that divide the line segment in three equal parts are called as points of trisection of the segment.)
solution:
[Textbook note: while dealing with point Q the book prints "\(\dfrac{AQ}{QD} = \dfrac{2}{1}\)"; there is no point D in this figure and the ratio meant is \(\dfrac{AQ}{QB} = \dfrac{2}{1}\). The working and the answers are unaffected.]

Let points P and Q be the points of trisection of the line segment joining the points A and B.

Point P and Q divide line segment AB into three parts.

AP = PQ = QB  .......... (I)

\(\dfrac{AP}{PB} = \dfrac{AP}{PQ + QB} = \dfrac{AP}{AP + AP} = \dfrac{AP}{2AP} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)  .......... From (I)

Point P divides seg AB in the ratio 1 : 2.

\(x\) co-ordinate of point P \(= \dfrac{1 \times (-7) + 2 \times 2}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{-7 + 4}{3} = \dfrac{-3}{3} = -1\)

\(y\) co-ordinate of point P \(= \dfrac{1 \times 4 + 2 \times (-2)}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{4 - 4}{3} = \dfrac{0}{3} = 0\)

Point Q divides seg AB in the ratio 2 : 1.  \(\therefore \dfrac{AQ}{QB} = \dfrac{2}{1}\)

\(x\) co-ordinate of point Q \(= \dfrac{2 \times (-7) + 1 \times 2}{2 + 1} = \dfrac{-14 + 2}{3} = \dfrac{-12}{3} = -4\)

\(y\) co-ordinate of point Q \(= \dfrac{2 \times 4 + 1 \times -2}{2 + 1} = \dfrac{8 - 2}{3} = \dfrac{6}{3} = 2\)

\(\therefore\) co-ordinates of points of trisection are \((-1, 0)\) and \((-4, 2)\).
note: The book prints "AQ/QD = 2/1" where it means AQ/QB — there is no point D in Fig. 5.18. Recorded as an errata bracket; the derivation and both answers are correct.

slope of line PQ \(= \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \dfrac{2 - 3}{1 - (-2)} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\)

stem: If slope of the line joining points P(k, 0) and Q(\(-3\), \(-2\)) is \(\dfrac{2}{7}\) then find \(k\).
solution:
P(k, 0) and Q(\(-3\), \(-2\))

Slope of line PQ \(= \dfrac{-2 - 0}{-3 - k} = \dfrac{-2}{-3 - k}\)

But slope of line PQ is given to be \(\dfrac{2}{7}\).

\(\therefore \dfrac{-2}{-3 - k} = \dfrac{2}{7}\)  \(\therefore k = 4\)

stem: If A(6, 1), B(8, 2), C(9, 4) and D(7, 3) are the vertices of \(\square ABCD\), show that \(\square ABCD\) is a parallelogram.
solution:
You know that Slope of line \(= \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}\)

Slope of line AB \(= \dfrac{2 - 1}{8 - 6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)  .......... (I)

Slope of line BC \(= \dfrac{4 - 2}{9 - 8} = 2\)  .......... (II)

Slope of line CD \(= \dfrac{3 - 4}{7 - 9} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)  .......... (III)

Slope of line DA \(= \dfrac{3 - 1}{7 - 6} = 2\)  .......... (IV)

Slope of line AB = Slope of line CD  .......... From (I) and (III)

\(\therefore\) line AB \(\parallel\) line CD

Slope of line BC = Slope of line DA  .......... From (II) and (IV)

\(\therefore\) line BC \(\parallel\) line DA

Both the pairs of opposite sides of the quadrilateral are parallel

\(\therefore \square ABCD\) is a parallelogram.
